query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: X‐ray diffraction (XRD) analysis performed after high-temperature wear testing can effectively capture the oxidation behaviour and phase stability of the high-entropy alloy via detection of protective oxide phases.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a dense multiphase microstructure achieved by inert gas atomisation and spark plasma sintering.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the sample to high-temperature reciprocating wear tests followed by XRD analysis of the wear tracks.
generation.conditions: Wear tests carried out at elevated temperatures (especially at 800 °C and 900 °C) under ambient atmospheric conditions for a defined duration.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer (spinel phase, similar to MgAl2O4) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: High temperatures promote oxidation during wear testing, which facilitates the formation of a stable, protective oxide film. This film is detectable by XRD through its characteristic diffraction peaks and correlates with improved wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures, XRD analysis will reveal strong spinel oxide phase peaks corresponding to the protective film formation, and this will correlate with increased wear resistance compared to samples tested at lower temperatures.
generation.baseline: The baseline state is established from room temperature or lower temperature (e.g., 22 °C and 500 °C) tests where little or no formation of the spinel phase is observed.
generation.boundary: The method’s effectiveness may be influenced by factors such as testing duration, actual processing-induced microstructure (e.g., contributions from minor phases like σ-phase), and subtle oxidation kinetics differences.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the role of additional phases (e.g., σ-phase) in overall oxidation behaviour, and whether similar oxidation mechanisms would prevail in other high-entropy alloy systems or under different wear conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 HEA samples. Conduct reciprocating wear tests under controlled conditions at a range of temperatures (e.g., 22 °C, 500 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C). After testing, perform XRD analysis on the wear tracks to assess the presence and intensity of oxide phases. Additionally, include control samples exposed to the same thermal conditions without mechanical wear.
measurements: XRD patterns to identify and quantify oxide phase peaks (e.g., spinel phase)
Coefficient of friction and hardness measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the XRD analysis does not show increased formation of the spinel oxide phase at higher temperatures, or if the oxide phase formation does not correlate with improved wear resistance when compared to lower-temperature tests or control samples, then the hypothesis that XRD analysis after high-temperature wear testing is an effective method for studying oxidation behaviour and phase stability is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
